title: Investing: Private credit warning over housing downturn
full_text:
Three interest rates increases this year have created a more difficult environment for Australian private credit investors, who have significant exposure to real estate developers now facing higher construction costs at the same time as sentiment in the property market weakens.
That's the warning from Wall Street investment giant Morgan Stanley, who said there was "limited transparency" about the loans made by local private credit firms, with the outlook "determined by the pass-through of construction cost inflation to developer margins and feasibility" and interest rates.
The comments, in a note by analyst Sharmeel Suka, came as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she was more concerned about the level of transparency and growing risks among private credit firms in the US, where the industry is far larger and has been under pressure as investors pull their funds.
Bullock, who was speaking at the RBA's press conference on Tuesday, said the big worry was that "people don't know where the leverage is".
"They don't know who is exposed," she said.
Documents released by the RBA following freedom of information requests this year showed the central bank has been bracing for mounting defaults across the sector and was concerned that any financial shock would be exacerbated by the high concentration of property loans among funds.
The documents also revealed the RBA was worried about the fallout from a rupture in overseas private credit, such as the collapse of a major fund. Asked directly about the documents for the first time, Bullock said there was "not a massive worry" about Australian private credit firms when compared to those in the US.
"I think the concern - and it's not just in the US, it's a bit in Europe as well - is that there's very little data on it," she said. "Any time that there's a big unknown ... [where there is] a big chunk of lending, but you don't know anything about it, that just makes people worried."
In the US, fears about bad loans made by private credit firms, which charge higher interest than banks because the borrowers are deemed riskier, have triggered redemption request from funds run by some of the biggest players in the industry, including Blue Owl Capital and BlackRock. Investors asked to withdraw $US29.5 billion ($42 billion) in the first half of the year alone.
The exodus has prompted some funds to limit withdrawals - typically to 5 per cent of assets - although executives have argued that the market has overreacted and is too sensitive to headlines, with returns unaffected.
The Wall Street Journal reported at the weekend that loan defaults at funds overseen by American investment giants Ares Management, Blackstone, Blue Owl and others had reached their highest levels since 2021.
In Australia, concerns have grown amid financial strains at major Sydney developer Bathla Group. The company is heavily backed by a number of private credit funds, and owes more than $3 billion. SQM Research, a ratings agency widely used by financial advisors, told clients it was concerned that one of Bathla's biggest backers, the Centuria Bass Credit Fund, had changed its rules to lend to the developer and was now uninvestable.
In turn, that led to Morningstar warning there could be a "wave of redemptions" at the Centuria-operated fund.
Morgan Stanley's Suka told clients that in addition to the "challenging environment" for the private credit sector from interest rate rises and higher energy prices after the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in late February, "data consistency" remained an issue for investors.
"Direct property and development may face margin compression from rising input costs that may impair borrowers' ability to service debt," he said.
The Australian private credit sector has grown to an estimated $250 billion as institutional and individual investors have chased higher yields and stable asset values by investing in funds that loan money to businesses.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has been sounding the alarm about private credit's heavy exposure to property construction. It previously estimated that half of the market was invested in real estate, with failed projects quickly compounding into serious issues for some funds.
The RBA, according to the documents released this year, flagged the heavy exposure of local private credit funds to property and construction, warning that shocks could flow from a "housing price crash, or sustained increase in construction costs", which were notable concerns for the economy.
ANZ on Tuesday said it expected house prices to fall 4.3 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027, driven by a 14.5 per cent fall in house prices in Sydney and a 12.8 per cent decline in Melbourne. Those drops have come after three interest rate increases, and amid Labor's changes to tax concessions.
Despite those worries, Bullock said this week that Australia's private credit industry was but a small part of the broader lending market.
"It's the banks that drive a lot of it, even in housing and business lending. It's still pretty small, the non-bank financial institutions," she said.
